source.title: Inducing human-like biases in moral reasoning LMs
source.authors: Artyom Karpov; Austin Meek; Bogdan Ionut Cirstea; SCho

record.tranche_reason: The study reports model-to-human-fMRI brain scores, not similarity between independently trained models or any other version of the claim.
record.gate_note: The post discusses prior brain-model alignment work and reports its own brain-score results. These measure correspondence to human fMRI data, not the inter-model convergence named in the claim; they are recorded as findings that fit no version. ETHICS accuracy results are not rows because they do not measure representational convergence.
record.test_reason: The post's own results are ETHICS accuracy and model-to-human-fMRI brain scores (encoding-model Pearson correlation). Neither compares the representations of independently trained models, seeds, modalities or features across models. The convergence literature appears only in the introduction, cited as LM-brain similarity motivation, so the post neither tests nor uses any version of the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors found no significant improvement in ETHICS accuracy or brain score from fMRI fine-tuning, apart from a small within-error gain for bert-large. They call this an update on the task's difficulty, not strong evidence that neuroimaging data cannot help alignment.
record.recipe_differences: The study does not apply a method for measuring inter-model convergence.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning BERT-family encoders on ETHICS and/or moral fMRI data did not significantly raise brain scores over pre-trained models (e.g. deberta 0.271 vs 0.264–0.273). Across the three models, brain score does not track size monotonically: roberta-large is lowest at 0.173 and deberta-v2-xlarge highest at 0.271.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Supervised fine-tuning on a small moral-reasoning fMRI dataset does not increase LM-to-brain representational correspondence beyond pre-trained levels.

record.problems: The authors describe the attempt as inconclusive and note preprocessing, data, model-selection, and fine-tuning difficulties. They state that there were few calculations for some pre-trained brain-score comparisons, which contributed to their error range. Their reported brain-score measure is model-to-human-fMRI correspondence rather than inter-model representational similarity.
record.rows_left_out: Layer-wise brain-score comparisons in Figures 3 and A10–A17 are described qualitatively but are not separately extracted because they do not measure any claim version; the post gives no individual layer values in the supplied text. ETHICS accuracy and sampling-method accuracy results are left out because they measure task performance, not representational convergence.

untested.parts: All: no inter-model similarity is measured as a function of scale.
All: no model-to-model mapping or stitching.
All: no cross-model features or circuits.
All: no inter-model alignment levels or causes.

record.verdict_notes: Relation changed from 'discusses' to 'cites_only'. The convergence literature (LMs converging on brain-like representations) is cited only as motivation and is not argued about. Brain-model alignment is outside every listed version, since the versions concern alignment between models. Brain scores have large σ (about 0.1) and few runs for the pre-trained condition, as the authors note in the comments.

versions.untested_parts: Whether independently trained models become more aligned as size or capability increases.
Cross-modal alignment between vision and language models on paired images and captions.
Feature or subspace convergence across random seeds.
Mapping or stitching representations between models, including linear maps or unpaired methods.
Recurrence of interpretable features or circuits across models.
Dependence of inter-model convergence on similarity metrics, settings, or input distributions.
Whether inter-model alignment is incomplete, plateaus, or is explained by shared data or objectives.
